en: The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Huanglong Huinan.

When the Master first took up residence at Chongsheng Chan Monastery in Tong’an, on the day he ascended the hall, after the proclamations of the petitions were finished, the Master held up the incense and said:
"This one offering of incense is for..."
May the Imperial Majesty’s sacred longevity be infinite.
Again, he offered incense, saying:
"This is for the Military Commissioner Langzhong and his civil and military officials."
May it extend blessings and longevity;
furthermore, may the realm be peaceful and secure,
and the Wheel of Dharma turn perpetually.
Again, he held up the incense and said,
"Tell me, assembly,
what is this single stick of incense?"
For whom should one act?
How many people have speculated on this,
yet remain ignorant of where it ultimately leads?
Today, for the sake of Chan Master Ciming of Hunan,
I have burned this single incense stick,
causing its fragrance to pervade all the monasteries throughout the world.
It shall become a calamity and a misfortune for all monastics.
The rector strikes the gavel and says:
"The assembly of dragons and elephants at this Dharma feast should contemplate the primary truth.
The Master sighed and said:
What a fine First Principle!
It was perfectly intact,
yet it has just been broken into two pieces by the Rector.
"Is there anyone who can continue this?
He then looked around at the assembly and said:
If you cannot connect them,
it will be like Tong’an today:
taking the head and making it the tail.
To take the tail for the head is a mistake.
Should anyone come forward with a question,
you must truly keep your eyes open.
At that time, a monk asked:
"The precious seat has already been ascended upon the Phoenix Ridge;
who shall succeed you in propagating the ancestral style?"
The Master drew a circle and said,
"The lineage of Shishuang has spread into Jiangxi. The student stepped forward and said, "It has indeed burst forth into Jiangxi."
The Master said:
"The bright sun is at its zenith,
yet the blind man feels his way on the ground."
Question: "What is the realm of Tongan?
The Master said:
"It cannot be seen."
The student asked,
"What is it like to be a person within the realm?
The Master said:
Faceless. One who asks is not a master if they do not "crack" and "peck";
one who "cracks" and "pecks" is not a master.
The great assembly gathered at the dais and requested that the Master meet them as a true adept.
The Master lowered one foot.
Jin said:
"Seeking flying snow within flames;
water beneath while fire burns the heavens."
The Master then withdrew his feet.
He stepped forward and said,
"The great assembly bears witness to this true spiritual friend."
The Master said,
"Tongan does not take advantage; you,
Dharma brother, do not take advantage either."
The student said, "This is something used by both houses;
what about 'seizing the drum and capturing the banner'?
The Master threw down his whisk.
The Master then said:
"Before I have even ascended this seat,
there is not a single thing."
As soon as I have ascended this seat, there are already many questions and answers.
I venture to ask the assembly: [what do you say?]
Suppose there were only a single question and a single answer;
would that still constitute the essential doctrine (zongcheng)?
If you say it does, [then consider this:]
Within the entire great treasury of the teachings,
how could there not be questions and answers?
For what reason do you say this?
A separate transmission outside the teachings,
handed down to those of the highest faculties;
if one says this is not appropriate, [one is mistaken].
What was the purpose of all those questions and answers just now?
A traveler on the path should open his own eyes.
Do not allow yourself to regret this later.
As for discussing this matter,
it is not something that can be reached through the powers of supernatural attainments or meditative realization.
This is not something discussed by those of mere erudition or intellectual wisdom;
the Buddhas of the three periods of time have said only that it is known by oneself.
The entire great treasury of the teachings cannot fully explain it.
Therefore, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, among the hundreds of thousands of myriads of beings, [only a few attained realization].
Only Kāśyapa was granted the privilege of hearing it directly;
at Huangmei, seven hundred eminent monks were entrusted with the robe and bowl by the Practitioner.
How could it be that you, driven by greed,
lust, folly, and attachment, consider victory and defeat to be your strength?
Truly, those who have left the household life—
One must rely on the resolute will of a great man to cut off both ends and return home to sit in peace.
Thereafter, he opened wide the gates and doors,
brought forth his own household wealth,
and received all who came and went.
Only by providing relief to those who are orphaned and destitute can one repay even a small portion of the Buddha’s profound kindness;
were it otherwise, [one would fail].
"This is impossible.
He struck the meditation seat with his whisk and descended from the seat,
whereupon he offered his formal expression of gratitude.
On New Year’s Day, he ascended the hall.
A monk asked,
"Not seeking after the various sages..."
Not valuing one's own spiritual nature is not yet the business of a patch-robed monk. What,
then, is the business of a patch-robed monk?
The Master said,
"In thirty years,
I have rarely encountered such a question."
The student said,
"In that case, would it not be failing the various sages?
The Master said:
He did not answer a word.
How could one say he was guilty?
The monk clapped his hands once.
The Master said:
"Hūṃ! To let this pass would be unacceptable."
The Master then said:
"As the four images shift and transform,
they end and begin again."
The harmony between the two polarities is truly realized at this auspicious time;
amidst the manifold complexities of conventional truth,
each follows the rites of mutual exchange.
The realm of True Suchness (tathatā) is not distinguished by being new or old. Why is this?
Have you not heard the Way?
"In a single thought, one universally contemplates immeasurable kalpas;
there is no going, no coming, and no abiding."
Since coming and going have been severed,
what "new" or "old" could there be?
Since it is neither new nor old, [what is there to be attained?]
Furthermore, why is there any need for prostrations or congratulations?
To go back and forth specifically for such things is unnecessary;
one need only maintain constant stillness within a single thought-moment.
Spontaneously, the three temporal limits are forgotten in their profound depth;
how can one be constrained by coming and going?
How can one inquire about the new and the old?
Therefore it is said:
"Thus understanding the matters of the three periods of time,
one transcends all expedient means and accomplishes the ten powers."
After a long silence, he said:
"Such a proclamation as this is known by everyone."
If one breaks two into three,
how many can there possibly be? Why is this so?
People of that time understood only how to hoist the sails with a following wind;
they did not understand how to pull the ropes against the wind.
[The Master] struck his meditation seat and descended from it.
Ascending the hall, he said:
"The winter solstice and the one hundred and fifth day of the cold food festival—
let us not speak of them."
Venerable Elders,
how would you explain this single phrase: "Thread the needle at midnight"?
If you can obtain it,
return my first tally to me;
if you cannot obtain it, [then speak].
Both sides suffer loss.
[The Master] descends from his seat.
He ascends the hall and says:
The Dharmakāya is without marks;
it manifests forms in response to sentient beings.
Prajñā is without cognition.
Illuminating in accordance with conditions,
he then held up his whisk and said,
"The whisk is held up."
This is called the Dharma-body;
is this not manifesting form in response to things?
The whisk comes sweeping across.
"This is called Prajñā.
Is this not 'illumination according with conditions'?
Thereupon, he laughed heartily.
Suddenly, someone came out and grabbed him;
Tong’an spat once and gave him a slap.
He overturned the meditation seat and dragged [the master] down the steps;
one cannot blame him for this.
Now that you lack such hands and feet for biting pigs and dogs,
Tongan has instead turned this command upside down.
[He] descends from the seat.
He ascended the hall and gathered the assembly.
After a long silence, he said:
"The carp is in its deep abode."
The solitary bird stood for a long time.
[The Master] struck the meditation seat and descended from it,
then ascended the hall and said:
Today is the eighth day of the fourth month,
the anniversary of our Buddha’s birth.
All the monasteries under heaven—
Everyone bathed the Buddha;
I remember this.
Zun Puna was among the assembly at Yaoshan.
While serving as the temple administrator during the ritual of bathing the Buddha,
Yaoshan asked him:
"You have only been able to bathe this one.
Can you also bathe that one?
Zun replied:
"Bring that one here.
Yaoshan then ceased [speaking].
The Master said:
The ancients, according to the occasion, would offer but a single word or half a phrase,
yet there was nothing clever about it;
nowadays, people exhaust their mental and physical efforts to arrange and construct [their speech].
In the end, they never reached his realm.
Among the assembly, some deliberated, saying,
"This is a bronze statue."
Which one is the Dharma-body?
A bronze statue has form;
it can be washed and cleansed.
The Dharmakāya is signless;
how can it be washed?
Yaoshan only knows one aspect of this.
Not knowing the second part,
he was caught off guard by Master Zun,
until his mouth was left hanging like a flat carrying pole.
He could not overcome his shame and regret.
Furthermore, it is said that when the ancient sages posed questions,
they did so solely to test people.
When asked, "Which one?
he immediately said, "Bring that one here!
This is precisely following after sounds and chasing after forms.
He bit into his words and entangled him in his elaborate rhetoric;
seeing that he did not understand, Yaoshan [let him go].
Therefore, he simply ceased speaking.
It is further said:
"Yaoshan came in this manner."
Already there was no cause for it, yet you stirred up trouble;
you gouged a sore upon healthy flesh.
Master Zun did not see that this was an illness.
Yet they apply more burning moxa over the scars of previous moxibustion.
Some say that the ancients had already attained [realization].
Acting as the occasion requires;
there is nothing acceptable and nothing unacceptable.
What is high? What is low?
Each knows that the other exists;
it is only from this point onward that later people have forcibly created distinctions.
The Master said:
As previously explained,
it is simply because one has not encountered the right person;
once the source is lost, [the path is severed].
To be deluded and fail to return is to rely solely on the sincere mind while engaging in calculation and deliberation.
To take this as the vehicle of our own school is truly not to know that it involves conceptualization and volitional effort.
Arising from the state of having a mind,
one employs this contemplation to discern the realm of the Buddha.
It is like attempting to burn Mount Sumeru with a firefly’s glow;
even if one were to pass through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust,
it could never catch fire.
Therefore, those who travel as seekers must by all means examine themselves regarding the matters handed down from of old.
How is it? Ultimately, with what will you confront birth and death?
Do not rely on a mere modicum of superficial and coarse intellectual views.
"You are creating an obstacle for yourself.
The Dharma of the Buddha is not a matter such as this.
Today, Tong’an does not shrink from the karma of speech."
I have explained this to everyone:
these two venerable masters,
one emerges and one enters.
The victory or defeat has not yet been seen.
Thirty years hence,
you must not err in your raising [of the question].
The assembly descends from their seats.
On the occasion of the Emperor’s birthday, he ascends the hall and says:
"Today is the anniversary of the Emperor’s birth."
Throughout the entire realm and under the vast heavens, all offer prayers for the prolongation of Your Majesty’s life;
this is indeed not without reason.
O virtuous ones!
Do you still recognize the Prince?
If one can recognize him,
then all the lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions are known.
All belong to the Elder;
they are nothing else.
Thus, one immediately sits within the city of Nirvana.
Reigning with effortless dignity,
he takes the three realms as his home and serves as the refuge for beings of the four modes of birth.
If you still do not understand,
burn incense within the Buddha Hall and join your palms at the main gate.
Descending from his seat,
he ascended the hall.
This was because a monk had delivered a letter.
He then recommended Master Si,
ordering Shitou to deliver a letter to Master Let of Mount Nanyue.
He immediately said,
"Turn around!
Come, I will give you a blunt axe to go live in the mountains."
Shitou went to Master Rang’s place;
before he had even arrived, Shitou presented the letter and asked:
"Seeking nothing from the various sages..."
"How can one be when not valuing one's own spiritual nature?
Letting replied,
"Your question is too lofty."
"Why do you not ask further? Shitou said,
"It would be better to undergo the cycle of saṃsāra for eternal kalpas."
"One does not seek liberation by following the various sages.
Master Rang did not respond;
Shitou then turned back.
Master Si asked,
"Not long after you left,
did the letter reach?"
Shitou said,
"Even faith does not penetrate;
even a letter does not reach."
Master Si said,
"For what reason?
Shitou then recounted the previous conversation.
He spoke again, saying:
"On the day I departed,
I was granted by the Master the promise of a single adze for dwelling upon the mountain."
He immediately requested,
"I pray that Master Si will lower one foot.
Shitou then prostrated himself.
He departed to enter Mount Nanyue and dwell among the mountains.
The Master said,
"Shitou has sent a letter."
This has been heard by all throughout past and present;
yet because later generations have not been skillful regarding its fundamental source,
few have been able to proclaim it.
This causes water and milk not to be distinguished,
and jade and stone not to be differentiated;
today, Tong’an has split them apart by half.
He bestowed [this] upon the great assembly.
Although Shitou was indeed capable of swift mastery,
he did not disgrace the tradition of his lineage.
Alas, in his eagerness to display his brilliance,
he was unaware that he had missed the essential point.
Since he has missed the essential point, [what can be done?]
Why is it that upon returning, you instead obtained the "rusty axe" for dwelling in the mountains?
If you can see into this here,
not only will you dwell in the mountains.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions,
in every atom and every land,
even within tiger dens and demonic palaces.
These are all places of abiding.
If you have not yet seen this,
I venture to say that none of you have yet found a place to settle your body and establish your life.
The assembly descended from their seats.
He ascended the hall and cited Master Yunmen, who said:
"On the level ground there are countless dead people;
one who can pass through the thorn forest is a true adept.
He then picked up his whisk and said:
"Great assembly,
if you call this a whisk,
it is truly a dead man on level ground."
"If you do not call it a whisk,
you have not yet penetrated the thicket of thorns.
[He] struck the meditation seat.
Descend from the seat.
Ascend the hall.
He gives a shout and says:
The entire earth was shattered like crumbling walls and melting ice by Tong'an’s single shout; you all— !
Where do you turn?
Where do you put on your clothes and eat your food?
If you have not yet found the place where one puts on clothes and eats food...
You must find a place where you can wear clothes and eat food.
If you recognize this place of wearing clothes and eating food,
it would be well to recognize your own nostrils.
Descending from his seat,
he ascended the hall and said:
"The vast waves roll on boundlessly."
White waves surge to the heavens;
those who have cut across the current and reached the shore sit upright,
having forgotten all anxieties.
A traveler in a solitary boat with a short oar,
frowning as he advances or retreats—
tell me, what is this?
"The wind is calm and the waves are still"—
how do you say it?
Is there anyone who can say it?
"If no one can attain the Way,
I shall bestow it as a gift upon all of you.
After a long silence, he said:
The fisherman sings leisurely to himself;
the woodcutter sings his song alone.
[He] descends from his seat.
Record of the Master’s Installation at Guizong. When the Master first entered the temple, he ascended the hall and said:
"I have come to Guizong Temple."
This is a great river of dhyāna.
Since it is a river of dhyāna,
how could there be no fisherman?
"Is there anyone who would like to ask a question?
After a long pause, as no one asked anything,
the Master departed.
Though many have horns, few are the *xiezhai* (unicorn-like creatures);
though feathers abound, rare are the *yuanyang* (mandarin ducks).
Indeed, the subtle and wondrous Dharma-body—
Therefore, one hears yet does not hear;
one sees yet does not see.
This is the pure, teacherless wisdom.
How could it be attained through thought,
or mastered through study? Yet,
were it not for the guidance of a teacher’s proclamation, [it would remain unattained].
Who can distinguish the origins of the schools without questions and answers?
Who can clarify what is heterodox and what is orthodox?
Now, when the Elder ascends the hall to give his discourse,
there is no one among the assembly who asks a question.
Since no one asks a question, [the discourse proceeds].
Furthermore, there is no one who provides an answer.
By what means can the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox be clarified?
If there were someone capable of distinguishing between the heterodox and the orthodox, [then it would be possible].
He came out, pushed over the meditation seat,
and shouted to disperse the assembly,
thereby venting his indignation on behalf of the monks.
If you cannot discern it now,
there will be new branches again next year;
the spring wind that brings such vexation shall never cease.
The assembly took their seats.
Ascending the hall, he said:
"The mani jewel is in the palm of your hand."
It divides its brilliance according to various colors;
like a precious moon suspended in the sky,
it reflects its image across a thousand rivers.
O virtuous ones,
a single question and a single answer;
a single blow of the staff and a single shout.
This is light and shadow;
one bright, one dark;
one seizing, one releasing.
These are shadows and reflections.
The mountains, rivers, and the great earth are shadows and reflections.
The sun, moon, and stars are shadows and reflections.
The entire Great Canon of the Buddhas of the three periods of time,
as well as all the great patriarchs and the elder monks throughout the land.
At the gate and in the courtyard, there is clashing and knocking;
though there are a thousand differences and ten thousand distinctions,
they are all but reflections and shadows.
Now tell me, what is the pearl?
What is the moon?
If you do not recognize the pearl and the moon, [you have missed the point].
To fixate on thoughts and words,
or to cling to light and shadows,
is like entering the ocean to count its sands.
To grind a tile to make a mirror,
hoping for its proper number and desiring its brightness—
this can by no means be achieved.
Have you not seen it said:
"If one extensively seeks the meaning of the texts,
it is like seeking a form within a mirror."
To further cease thought and contemplate emptiness is much like grasping at the moon in water;
when a patch-robed monk reaches this point, [he must transcend it].
There must be a path for turning the body.
If you can turn it, then you may spread them out or gather them together.
There is nothing that is not the Great Matter manifesting before one;
moving freely in all directions,
there is no further dharma remaining.
If you cannot turn it around,
you are like an old crow in a cloth bag;
though alive, you are as good as dead.
I am but an ordinary man of the mountain wilds,
naturally lacking in learning or insight.
Yesterday, I was graced by the presence of the Imperial Secretary and Vice-Governor of this prefecture.
I have been specially summoned;
however, as one under the jurisdiction of my provincial fief,
I dare not fail to come.
Only as he was about to reach the gate did he receive the command to return to Guizong;
he reflected upon his conduct and deliberated whether to advance or retreat.
I am deeply grateful and feel greatly humbled.
This is none other than the Palace Aide and Judicial Official,
who in the past received a prophecy from the Buddha.
Manifesting as a royal minister,
he constantly devoted himself to reverently upholding the teachings of the Awakened Hero during his leisure from the administration of government affairs.
I wish for the breeze of wisdom to fan alongside the wind of Yao,
and hope that the sun of the Buddha will shine as brightly as the sun of Shun;
this would truly be nothing less than setting one's heart upon the welfare of living beings.
Why is it that you have exerted yourself with such sincerity?
On this day, you were once again graced by the imperial canopy’s visit to this Dharma assembly,
ensuring its completion from beginning to end.
I am deeply honored by these kind words.
In the past, when the Prime Minister Pei held office in the imperial court,
Huangbo was recognized and supported by him.
Han Yu’s fame was preeminent in his own day;
Da Jian attained mastery of the Way.
Judging the present by the past, [the two are comparable].
What difference is there?
I wish to speak further,
yet I fear it would weary those who listen.
The assembly descends from their seats.
He ascends the hall and says:
"I shall now lift up the essential principles for all."
Neither ordinary nor holy,
he opens up a single thread of a path;
there is something to be deliberated upon.
He then picked up his staff and said,
"Right now, as this staff stands upright,
the entire ten-direction world stands upright at once."
Again, holding his staff horizontally, he said:
"Right now the staff is held horizontally;
the worlds of the ten directions are all simultaneously horizontal."
Why is this? It is because one has not seen that the ultimate small is identical to the great.
Forgetting and severing all boundaries,
the great reaches to the small;
one perceives neither limit nor exterior.
[The Master] struck his staff and descended from the seat.
The Censor-in-Chief entered the mountain and ascended the seat.
A monk asked:
"The Provincial Commissioner Chaogai has traveled from afar to attend this Dharma assembly."
"Regarding the upward-tending vehicle of the patriarchal tradition,
I beg the Master for a single instruction.
The Master said:
[He wears] a single-character head-wrap and a hat with a pointed brim.
He enters and says:
"Not only does the Circuit Intendant benefit from this goodness."
The student prostrated to express gratitude for the teacher’s kindness.
The teacher said,
"I have pulled out your eyebrows."
"I have knocked off your nostrils.
What do you say to that?
The monk sighed.
The Master said:
"To make flour, one must use the wheat of that very province;
to sing the song, one must be a person from the imperial capital."
The Master then said:
"The root of sentient beings relies upon the ocean of wisdom as its source."
The stream of sentient beings takes the Dharmakāya as its very substance;
it is only because emotions arise that wisdom becomes obstructed.
In daily life, one acts without awareness;
thoughts transform and the physical body differs.
Following the karmic conditions of one's inclinations, one fails to return; thus, past and present are vast and boundless.
Who understands the fundamental cause?
One busies oneself with love and hatred;
the source of emotion is illusory and false.
Therefore, I, Śākyamuni, the Tamer,
have long since realized Bodhi;
yet I take pity on those of us who, through weary toil, bring about our own cyclic wandering.
Thereafter, having attained great wisdom,
he manifested a body of wondrous marks and dwelt in the world for forty-nine years.
He expounds the twelvefold teachings,
establishing gates of transformation according to the sharpness or dullness of their faculties.
May those of superior, middling, and inferior faculties each attain their gradual progress.
It is like the great ocean, which does not refuse even the smallest stream.
Even if mosquitoes, gadflies, or asura kings were to drink its water,
they would all become fully satiated.
Thereafter, as his period of transforming conditions was drawing to a close,
he manifested his passing beneath the twin śāla trees and addressed the great assembly of humans and devas, saying:
I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye,
the wondrous mind of Nirvana;
I entrust it to Mahākāśyapa.
A separate transmission outside the teachings,
handed down to those of superior faculties;
this Dharma cannot be understood through the conceptualization of deliberate mental effort.
It cannot be entered through the cultivation and realization of supernatural powers;
it cannot be known with a mind that has intentionality,
nor can it be attained with a mind that is devoid of intentionality.
To realize this is to transcend the three realms instantaneously;
to be deluded by it is to sink into oblivion for ten thousand kalpas.
It is just like the present universal assembly of kings and officials.
The monastics and the laity sat together at the same table;
their postures were solemn and dignified,
and their perception remained clear and undimmed.
Is this delusion or awakening?
One can perceive it within this very seeing,
without waiting for the completion of three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
When the merit of the myriad practices is perfected,
one thought-moment transcends all;
there is no longer any before or after.
On this day at the mountain temple, we are most fortunate.
We have humbly received the honor of the personal visit of the Provincial Surveillance Commissioner,
the Du Guan, and the Palace Secretary.
Having spent the night adorning the desolate monastery, I come to you with my greetings;
may you enjoy ten thousand blessings.
How much more so for these two honored officials,
who have long planted the roots of virtue and now manifest in the bodies of secular administrators.
By governing the people with benevolence and kindness,
you shall relieve the current Son of Heaven from the urgency of his sleepless nights and anxious days.
Whether monastic or lay,
noble or humble,
all shall receive its blessing of merit and longevity.
How can one adequately express this?
Having already been graced by your presence,
please also set aside your heavy concerns.
Therefore, our Buddha, the Tathāgata, said:
"As for those who preach the Dharma,
there is no preaching and no demonstrating."
Those who listen to the Dharma neither hear nor attain it;
furthermore, they hear.
Zhongni and Wenbo Xue had long desired to meet one another;
one day, they halted their carriage and encountered each other on the road.
Neither spoke a word;
each returned to his own quarters.
Later, a disciple asked:
For a long time, the Master had wished to see Wen Bo Xue;
yet when they met,
they did not exchange a single word.
"What is the meaning of this?
Zhongni said,
"When gentlemen meet one another..."
"The Way exists in the direct encounter.
Now tell me, when the ancients met,
how did the Way exist in that direct encounter?
Today this mountain monk beats the drum and ascends the hall;
to speak so insistently and purposefully is,
in truth, a total failure.
Descending from his seat,
he ascended the hall and said:
"To stroke a tiger's whiskers in accordance with its nature— one must surely look back at oneself."
Holding the snake’s tail upside down, let others guess;
a barbarian coming and a Han appearing are but ordinary matters.
Do not hang the bright mirror upon a high terrace.
The abbot descended from his seat and ascended the hall, saying:
"Upon the Peak of Purple Cloud, black clouds gather in dense masses."
In Lake Poyang, white waves surge to the heavens;
all arises from non-action,
and all occurs without being so intended.
If you further attempt to interpret this through conceptual deliberation,
it remains a vast distance of one hundred and eight thousand miles.
Descend from your seat.
Ascending the hall,
he held up his staff and said:
"Held horizontally or used upside down."
Pushing open Maitreya’s eyes,
light departs and darkness arrives, knocking down the patriarch’s nostrils.
At that very moment—
Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra held their breath and stifled their voices;
Linji and Deshan laughed out loud with "he-he.
But tell me, what was it they were laughing at?
"Hey! Descend from the seat.
[The Master] ascends the hall.
Once, a scholar came to visit Muzhou.
Muzhou asked him,
"What have you realized?"
The scholar said, "I am proficient in twenty-four styles of calligraphy.
The Master pointed a single dot in the air with his staff and said: "What style is this?"
"Do you understand?
The scholar was at a loss for words.
The State Governor said:
Furthermore, Daohui did not recognize the "Eight Strokes of the Character 'Yong'" (yǒngzì bāfǎ) in the writings of twenty-four masters.
The Master said:
Muzhou’s single point was already present before King Bhīṣmagarjitasvaranādin;
yet when it came to his treatise on the eight worldly dharmas,
he was exposed by a layman.
If one returns to the source, it is not so:
none of the disciples of Confucius recognized him;
the blue-eyed barbarian monk smiled and nodded his head.
Descending from his seat,
he ascended the hall and raised the following case: Master Yanyang asked Zhaozhou.
